subtopic: PROPOSED ALLOWANCES AT AGE SIXTY AND OVER
speechtext:
Yes, I know that; I realize quite well that conditions to-day are not exactly what they were in 1926. Two votes are perhaps not as important in this parliament as they were ten years ago. Nevertheless, I say again that we appreciate the kindly sentiments expressed on that occasion, and I do hope that the resolution now on the order paper will meet with the same sympathetic consideration. For, after all, a principle is the same, whether it is endorsed by a majority of two or of one hundred; and I assume the principle underlying the question of old age pensions is the same in 1936 as it was in 1926.
The scope of the present act is rather wide; it takes in, I believe, seven of the nine provinces of Canada. There are at present two provinces in which the old age pensions scheme has not yet become operative, but in those provinces where the act is an established fact we can regard that piece of legislation,

Retiring Allowances-Mr. Heaps
in my opinion, one of the most important in the way of social legislation which the house has ever enacted, as a permanent part of their social law's. I do not think any government, whatever its political complexion may be, will ever see fit to repeal the act once it has been in operation.
1 was rather surprised to discover that, in the seven provinces in which the scheme is in operation, there were prior to and including March 31 of last year, 101,051 persons in receipt of old age pensions. That number was exclusive, of course, of Quebec and New Brunswick. When those two provinces come under the provisions of the act we shall have, I am satisfied, a considerable addition to that number. I understand that in New Brunswick legislation is pending in that regard, and I am also led to believe that in Quebec legislation is likely to be introduced in the near future to extend to the old people of that province that long needed relief which I know many of them have been looking for in the past few years. The situation in Quebec at the present time is somewhat similar to the state of affairs that existed in this house in 1926; they have not a stable government there, so that the old people in that province are likely to come into their own at an early date.
The constitutional difficulties that have so often been thrown in the way of the passage of social legislation in Canada seem bo have been successfully overcome so far as old age pensions are concerned; and to-day, I am pleased to say, there is no question about the validity of this particular law in this country. Further, I think it can be asserted that, considering it was a new piece of legislation in this dominion, and presented difficulty in many ways because it was a dominion statute operated by provincial authorities, the act is working fairly well, with one or two exceptions which it is not necessary for me to go into at this time.
One point which during the past few years must, I think, have become obvious to practically every member, irrespective of his party affiliations, is the necessity for a much lower age limit than that which applies at the present time. I believe we must all regard seventy as too high an age limit for pension after a person has served the state in one form or another practically throughout his life. In other countries-and I am referring now to countries within the British empire-the age limit is much lower than it is in Canada. In Great Britain it is sixty-five, and in Australia it is sixty-five for males and sixty for females, while in certain instances, in the event of

incapacity, the age limit for men in that country is sixty. Practically the same age limit is in force in New Zealand; therefore it is much lower than it is in Canada.
There is to-day a very large volume of opinion, not merely in this country but in other parts of the world, in favour of reducing the age limit at which people receive pensions, not only because such a measure is humane, not only because it is an act of humanity to take care of the aged and the needy, but also on account of the problem confronting us from the economic standpoint-the problem of unemployment. In the last election the present leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) came ,out in favour of old age pensions at the age of sixty; he thought it would be a good thing. In the United States there is a large and growing body of opinion in favour of paying old age pensions at the age of sixty. I am not referring at the moment to what is commonly called the Townsend revolving plan; I am not sufficiently familiar with it to be able to discuss it at all. In addition to that plan, which is taking a firm hold on the people of the United States, we find one of the prospective candidates for the Republican nomination for president there, Mr. Borah, in favour of granting old age pensions at the age of sixty, the pension to be between fifty and sixty dollars a month.
The reasons that can	be given	why	weshould grant pensions to persons of sixty and over are very many, but I shall discuss only a few of them. To-day we are living in a competitive age, an age which is different from any former time. We are living under conditions that are different from anything we have known heretofore. The struggle for existence is becoming keener and keener, and men to-day at the age of sixty find themselves in a position in	which	it	is practically impossible for them because of their age to obtain the means of livelihood. In the second place, when a man has worked under such keen conditions as those under which he is compelled to work, he is practically of little value in the industrial field when he reaches the age of three score. There are very few employers of labour who employ men when they have reached the age of sixty. The consequence is that	when	a	man	hasreached that age he has	either	to	shift	for
himself as best he knows how, or become the recipient of either public or private charity. There is very little opportunity to-day for men to save out of their earnings anything to put away for what we may term a rainy day, or for old age. I know of many firms in this country who will not employ men when

Retiring Allowances-Mr. Heaps
they are even over forty years of age. At fifty, positions become extremely precarious, and at sixty it is almost impossible for men in these days to find work; in fact a man at sixty or over becomes a drug on the labour market.
We often ask ourselves the question: What is the nation's greatest asset? It has been asked in the house during the past few days. Some might say it is property; it is buildings, or it is natural resources, but I believe if we ponder the question a little further we shall arrive at the same conclusion, that the greatest asset we have in the Dominion of Canada is the people themselves, our Canadian people. Then, if we come to determine the question whether we should look after the rights of property or the rights of our Canadian people, I think our sympathies as well as our interests will lead us to assist the human beings who comprise our Canadian population. It is often stated that the individual has a duty to the state. I believe that, but at the same time I believe the state also has a duty toward the individual. For after a person has worked and given of his best during his life time to help in building up the country and making it a proper place to live in, when he reaches old age; when he has arrived at the age of sixty, he is entitled to receive something in return for his services. There ought to be between the state and the individual as reciprocal relationship which does not exist to-day. An individual can give of his best until he is sixty or sixty-five years old, and all of a sudden he finds that he is cut off without any means of subsistence. The duty of the state as well as that of the individual is to promote the well-being of all concerned. Is it fair to ask the individual at times so to humiliate himself or herself as to become the recipient of either public or private charity? We have at this time in the dominion 1,200,000 men, women and children in receipt of public relief. That figure does not take into account the vast number of men, women and children who are recipients of private relief in one form or another. There must be in these days a very large number of these people who are sixty years of age or over and who find themselves on the bread line through no fault of their own.
I think I can state with a certain amount of assurance that practically every hon. member would say he is sympathetic to the idea of pensioning people when they reach the age of sixty. But I suppose those same hon. members who will tell me they are favourable and sympathetic to this idea, will comt along wdth a very hoary and musty question: Where is the money to come from? If
the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) were in his seat, I would ask him whether we have in this country enough in the way of foodstuffs to give to all the people in Canada who are sixty and over, a reasonable amount by way of food, and I believe the minister would reply to me that we have more than sufficient for that purpose. Then, if I were to turn to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler), I would ask him, if he were here: Have we in this country sufficient clothing and shelter to satisfy all the reasonable requirements of our people over the age of sixty? I think I should receive from the hon. minister the answer that we have more than sufficient for those purposes. Then I would turn to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), whom I see in his seat, and I would say to him: Have you enough money to satisfy the requirements of those over the age of sixty? And I would be met with a most emphatic "No." There is the contradiction. Enough food, clothing and shelter in the Dominion of Canada to satisfy all the reasonable requirements of these people of sixty and over- no doubt, that would be admitted by the members of the government-and yet when it comes to trying to give to these people of sixty and over those requirements which in our corporate capacity we have produced in this country, we say: You cannot have them, because there is something that stands in the way of your being able to receive those things to which you probably have a right. When I ask the question whether the money will be forthcoming, knowing as I do that I shall receive that negative reply from the Minister of Finance, I feel like inquiring whether that same question was asked in the years 1914 to 1918, when this country spent approximately two billions of dollars. Was ever the question asked when that money was being spent, not to conserve or to preserve human life, but for the very reverse purpose:	Where is that money coming
from? The money was there for the very simple reason that we had its equivalent in the way of goods and services that we could give either to the people of this country or to those who required it. So if to-day we have in Canada the goods and services to maintain our population of sixty and over, there should be no difficulty, if only there is the will to do it, to find ways and means of providing for those people that reasonable standard of living which they have a right to expect. Between 1914 and 1918 approximately half a million people were taken out of productive work in this country, and were engaged in destructive work. Yet in spite of

Retiring Allowances-Mr. Heaps
the fact that half a million of the flower of the country's manhood were taken out of productive employment those who were left behind were able to maintain that half million in the work they were doing and to provide for themselves a decent standard of living. We can go even beyond that. During that period there was no shortage in Canada either of men or of money to carry on the work of the war.
If to-day everyone at the age of sixty were taken out of productive employment this would have a twofold effect:	First, it
would provide for people many of whom are hardly able to give a proper day's service in industry, and then it would give to our young people an opportunity to do some useful work, an opportunity which has been denied to thousands of them since they have left school.
The government also must find money with which to carry on the services of the country, and part of that money is obtained by borrowing. I remember very well-and I want to bring this incident to the attention of the house-that in the fall of 1930 we had a session of parliament lasting only a few weeks. We were called into session in order to provide the means of giving relief to large numbers of men and women who at that time were out of work. The government of the day came to the house and asked for a large appropriation, out of which $20,000,000 was set aside for the provision of food, clothing and shelter for the unemployed in Canada. What happened? The first thing done by the government of the day, as by both previous and subsequent governments, was to go to New York where they obtained a loan of $100,000,000. In the meantime there were vast numbers of people anxiously awaiting relief, but until such time as that money was obtained from the bankers of New York the people of Canada were unable to obtain the relief that was so badly required. The farmers of the west, together with the workers in the cities, had produced wealth in abundance, food, clothing and shelter; yet before our people could eat that food and before they could obtain that clothing and shelter we had to go to a foreign country for permission to do so. If there is anything more topsyturvy in our economic structure than a situation of that kind I should like to know where it may be found. In other words we must get permission from the bankers of New York before we can aat the foodstuffs we produce in our own country.
I realize,^ further, Mr. Speaker, that to give a pension of $50 a month, which is the sum I have in mind, to people sixty years

of age would probably require half the total revenue of the dominion. I know the minister could not afford that; I know it would require a vast sum of money, but we must bear in mind that this sum of money would go into circulation in this country in the purchase of food, clothing and shelter, because as a rule the workingman lives to the limit of his income, and the same would apply to those in receipt of a pension of $50 a month from the government. To take care of such a situation I am in favour of a limited form of controlled inflation. Some hon. members may be afraid of that. I know in Great Britain people thought the whole country was going to collapse when a few years ago it was feared that she was going off the gold standard. An election was fought and a government was returned on that issue, to keep Great Britain on the gold standard, but it was not long after that election before she went off the gold standard. In those countries which have gone off the gold standard and where there has been a limited form of inflation, nothing very serious has happened.
Perhaps at this point, while dealing with that aspect of the question, I might give the figures relating to the older population, as prepared for me by the bureau of statistics. In 1931 the number of these people in Canada was as follows:

When Quebec and New Brunswick come under the scheme, naturally that proportion will be materially increased; it may be nearer one-half than one-third. speechtext:
In any measure enacted by parliament there are always regulations saying who may be entitled to come under the act, and so it would be with a measure granting pensions at sixty. There are many people in executive and other positions who, at the age of sixty, might well be allowed to remain in their position, who would still find something to do. As I am pointing out, less than one-third of the people of over seventy years of age are receiving old age pensions at the present time, and we can base our arguments in connection with this matter on a somewhat similar mathematical calculation, except that on the average there would be fewer people requiring pensions at sixty than there would be at seventy. I think that is quite obvious, because at sixty a person has an opportunity of putting something away to provide for himself and those dependent upon him, but when he lives to the age of seventy, what he may have saved in the interval will have disappeared.
I am free to admit that this problem of old age is becoming more important as the years go by. Medical science has made such rapid strides that the average span of life has been greatly increased during the last few generations. Unfortunately the application of our economic laws has not kept pace with our knowledge and application of the laws of medical science, with the result that the percentage of our old people to-day is greater than it ever has been. I was surprised when I received these figures from the bureau of statistics, showing the large population of what I might call elderly people here in Canada.
Now we may speak of the cost.- Many things may be offset against that. At the present time it is costing us a large sum of money in the way of relief to maintain our people, to maintain them in institutions for the care of their health, or even in our penal institutions, for it has always been found that in times of unemployment penal institutions are filled to overflowing. I venture to say that if we set off against the cost of pensions at sixty the advantages that would be gained, the cost would be much less than it would at first appear to be. I mentioned a few minutes ago that in 1914 and the following years we spent approximately two billion dollars on a war in Europe and all that that entailed. The product of that war was little other than
misery. I believe few people in Canada would ever again be willing to have this country become a party to a war in Europe or anywhere else. But if we could afford to spend that enormous sum for human slaughter, disease, misery, and all that follows from war, does not the house think it is far better in this day to spend some money, not for the slaughter of human beings but in a war that will preserve life, a war against poverty and disease? May I quote what the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said recently; I do not do this very often. Speaking on the night of October 14, after the election results were known, he said:
The struggle for the rights of the people will, in the realm of economic liberty and security, be carried on as never before. Poverty and adversity, want and misery are the enemies which Liberalism will seek to banish from our land.
Those are fine sentiments; they sound even better to me because they were spoken after the election instead of before. I say to the Liberal party: Carry out to the very letter that statement of the Prime Minister. I want to see the Liberal party in this house war against those evils which the Prime Minister mentions, against poverty and adversity, and fight for the economic liberty and security of the masses of the people of this country. What security have they to-day? What security has the man of sixty, or even the man of fifty, to-day? None whatsoever. To-day, as I know and as most of us know, there are innumerable instances of men who have worked ten, fifteen, twenty years for a large corporation; then at a moment's notice a man may receive a slip stating, "Your services are no longer required," and he has to go out on the street and shift for himself as best he can. Yet these same large corporations use , horses and when those horses have done their work and are no longer required they are not told to go out and shift as best they can. No; they are kept in the stable; they are fed and sheltered for the rest of their days. It is in the very nature of our modem industrial life that these large corporations treat human beings much worse 'than they treat their old horses.
I may be told that the statement of the Prime Minister will be lived up to by the Liberal party. All I can say is that I hope they will do much better in future than they have so far. May I say to my friends of the Liberal party that although they won the last election by a very large majority they have not yet achieved victory. Far from it. Victory will be achieved by the Liberal party and by
320	COMMONS
Retiring Allowances-Mr. Wermenlinger
this parliament only when we have eliminated those conditions of which I have spoken, when we have given to the people of Canada that economic security, that liberty to which every Canadian citizen is entitled.
So far we have heard very little as to what the future policy of the government will be. We are told that it will be unfolded from time tp time during this and other sessions of parliament. I am free to admit that some of us are rather impatient; we want to know with as little delay as possible what the policy of the government is going to be in regard to giving our people that economic security which they have a right to expect. The mere lowering of trade barriers between this and other countries is not a remedy for the evils from which we are suffering, for if all the trade barriers between the nations of the world were thrown down to-morrow we should still have a tremendous unemployment problem. I do not believe in sending our foodstuffs and other goods of which we are supposed to have a surplus to other countries when our own people are compelled to go without them; we should first satisfy the needs of our own people. I say to the government: Adopt a bold and definite policy. If they do that they will receive the support not only of the small group I have the honour to represent in the house but of a large section of public opinion outside as well.
The motion I have proposed has a number of specific objectives. First, it aims to take out of industry people aged sixty and over and so give to the younger people the opportunity of doing something useful instead of being recipients of public relief. It aims at putting into the hands of the people a much larger volume of purchasing power than they have at present. For any minister or any hon. member to rise in his place and say that this or that is impracticable is not sufficient in the circumstances in which we live. We Look for something definite and positive from the government. If this is not the right way of going about what we seek to do I hope the government will show what is the right way. Instead of meeting this resolution with negative criticism I hope the house will deal with it constructively, and if this is not at least a partial way out of the difficulty I shall be only too happy to support something which will show better results.

member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps). I promise that my remarks will be brief.
The hon. member moved:
Whereas there exists in Canada an acute unemployment situation;
Every one realizes this fact and I, perhaps, more so than the majority of members in this house, owing to my association with the school board and city council of Verdun.
And whereas, it is desirable that as many as possible be absorbed into the useful industrial life of the dominion.
Such is the wish of all; however, a paragraph seems to be missing between the second and the last one. The hon. member for North Winnipeg concludes:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government be requested to immediately introduce legislation granting adequate retiring allowances-
I agree to this. In fact, in a greater degree than any other hon. member have I the privilege of representing in this house a constituency whose population is composed entirely of workers, who find themselves today in dire straits. However, I only wish that, between the second and third paragraphs of his resolution, the hon. member for North Winnipeg had inserted: "Unless work can be provided," either revenue-producing work, useful work or necessary work; for it might be dangerous, at present, to grant pensions to people over sixty years of age. I do not know, Sir, whether I am transgressing the rules of the house, but, representing a constituency made up in equal parts of people of English and of French descent, one half of which are artisans such as bricklayers, carpenters, joiners and plumbers, at present unemployed, the other half belonging to the so-called "white-collared brigade," it strikes me that, at this stage, our main object should be to provide legitimate and remunerative employment for our people.
I fully endorse the speech delivered yesterday by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church); I did not hear it in full, but I read it with pleasure in hansard. However, I am not ready to express an opinion on the questions of housing and of slum-clearance.
On behalf of the workers of my constituency may I say, Sir, to the hon. member for North Winnipeg that I should have preferred to find an additional clause in his resolution, between the second and third ones, for I agree with the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) and the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Miss Macphail) that it is work that our labouring classes seek. I shall not stress the point further, as I shall

Retiring Allowances-Mr. McLean (Meljort)
have an opportunity in the near future to deal more thoroughly with this important question of remunerative work.
May I point out that' during the past forty years Verdun has suffered from numerous floods; we have been constantly compelled, in order to protect ourselves, to raise the level of our embankments. These floods are due to works carried on by the dominion government down stream, either in Montreal harbour or at Victoria bridge, where the piling up of the ice in the spring raises the level of the water. Because of its low-lying ground, the city of Verdun is in a unique situation and has always suffered from floods. We have never asked for aid; we have perhaps shown ourselves too-self-sacrificing.

Let me read a few lines from this pamphlet *-and remember this is not a newspaper. The argument is intended to show that there is no way in the world whereby Canada can exchange her surplus commodities for the surplus commodities of other lands and so enjoy the benefit both of the things that nature has endowed us with in this country and the things that nature enables people in other countries to produce-people in other lands more favourably situated with respect to the production of certain commodities. I quote from page 13:
Every country has a surplus of almost the same kind of goods. There are no new countries left for capitalism to exploit. There is not in the entire world a foreign market sufficient to keep capitalism going. In other words, capitalism cannot exist without foreign markets and there are no foreign markets.
I would point out that in this paragraph "capitalism" is used interchangeably with "private ownership." There is no market for the things produced under private ownership; there is no market in the world for goods because too many goods have been produced or could be produced. And here is the proof-I quote:
Take, for instance, automobiles. Someone has estimated that the United States of America could make a sufficient number of automobiles to supply eight worlds the size of our world at the same ratio of users to the population of the eight worlds as now applies to users in the U.S.A. to-day in relation to the population of that country. With such a capacity output the U.S.A. must try to sell its automobiles to all the other countries of the world. But at the same ratio of users to population Canada can produce automobiles for three worlds the size of ours, so she must also try to sell her automobiles outside of Canada. Great Britain can make enough automobiles to serve five world's as large as our world, so she also must find a market; then France, Germany, Czechoslovakia and Japan, etc., can all make more automobiles than the world could use. Where, then, is the foreign market for automobiles? Obviously no such market exists, nor is there a foreign market for all the other commodities which are produced in common by the industrialized nations of the world.
I do not need to enter into any argument to convince the house that all industrialized countries have not the same kind of goods in the same abundance; and as my hon. friend has pointed out, even in Alberta, coal is not common under all circumstances and in all places, because he said some people there suffer from lack of that commodity in Alberta,

I realized at once the ridiculousness of the argument. If it were true, then the Liberal philosophy of trade and exchange would fall to the ground absolutely. If every country were self-contained, if every people had within their own surroundings all the wealth they needed, there would be no necessity for them to exchange anything with any other country; they could supply all their own requirements from within. If all industrialized countries had the same wealth in the same quantities, there would be no point in seeking to exchange one form of wealth for another, so long as men with health and intelligence cared to work.

The mover referred to that as the reason for the proposal. I have here a news item entitled, "Outlook hopeless for young people, says Garland,"-that is Mr. E. J. Garland, who was the representative of an Alberta constituency at the time this speech was reported. It says:
Mr. Garland emphasized the tragedy of the hopeless outlook for the rising generation, stating that the youths of to-day were being simply poured out into the world, with no prospect for any kind of jobs.
I submit in that case it was not fair to these people to say that there was positively no hope for the young people of the country. I submit there is much more hope for them to-day than if the socialist plan were adopted. I hold a chart of that plan in my hand. The idea is to put all the unemployed in the civil service, to divide society into seven groups-
-and the particiilar function of our price fixing and adjustment board is to fix the

remuneration for services rendered, to each of these groups of society so that an equilibrium may be maintained as nearly as it is humanly possible to do so.
In the civil service they would put the third group, and-
-this includes our unemployed, who are already maintained by society as a whole.
They are to be given the same remuneration as farmers, industrial workers and other people of this country.
I submit that the resolution before us is not wise, that no evidence has been submitted that it would be a good thing for the country or a good thing for the people. I said a while ago that many people of sixty feel that they are in the prime of their lives, that they are able to turn out better work than they were able to do before. I know that there are many over sixty among our returned men who have the right, perhaps, to expect more generous treatment than they are receiving at the present time. The law provides for them at sixty the same old age pensions as it provides for others at seventy, and it may be that it is desirable to extend special consideration to them; but to say that for all the workers who wish to retire, even if it were not compulsory to do so, adequate retiring allowances should be given, I think is a mistake.
We are sometimes told that the trouble with the world is that there is so much of everything we might have and that we are not using. I remember, and I wish to quote from memory, the words of one of the greatest economists in Europe to-day, Doctor Gustav Cassel, of Stockholm. He says: "We are told to-day that the trouble is that this is an age of plenty, that we cannot distribute it. It is not yet an age of plenty. In 1928, when production was at its height, when the factories were open for longer hours than they were before, and when the machines were running faster than they ever did before, we were turning out barely as much wealth as was required to satisfy the people of the world on the scale upon which they were accustomed to live at that time." That being true of 1928, when the wheels of industry were running at their fastest and when there were no unemployed at all who were able and willing to work, if this economist was correct-and I submit that there is no greater name in the economic science of Europe to-day-we were producing barely enough for the needs of the people on the scale to which they had become accustomed.

speechtext:
Just a moment and I will be through. Why is it, then, that to-day we are living on a poorer and lower scale? There are three principal reasons. One is that we are not producing the wealth we were producing at that time; we are not producing the amount of wealth this country could produce. Why is that so? One principal reason is the mistaken policies of this and many other countries that have not allowed us to exchange our surplus wealth in the markets of the world in order to bring home our wages. It is not enough to sell our wealth; we must be allowed an opportunty to bring home our wages in the form of goods o.r services we wish to buy from other countries, and during the last five years in particular in this and many other countries we have not been allowed to do so. There is another difficulty, to which I have already referred. Many governments have provided services at which our forefathers would have scoffed. These services may be and in some oases are desirable, but many of the things that have been done were neither imperative nor essential. That is another factor contributing to present conditions.
Now I want to give my hon. friend, who wished to ask a question, and who was courteous enough not to interrupt me, an opportunity to put his question.

subtopic: PROPOSED ALLOWANCES AT AGE SIXTY AND OVER
speechtext: If it is true that we are in an age of scarcity I should like to ask the hon. member why we do not put the unemployed to work to create more.

subtopic: PROPOSED ALLOWANCES AT AGE SIXTY AND OVER
speechtext:
That is a fair question, and I will try to answer it. It is absolutely true that to-day we are in an age of relative scarcity in Canada. Let me give an illustration. I was going to say that for the last five or six years providence has failed to shine, but that is not what providence has failed to do. Providence has failed to rain on southern Saskatchewan, Alberta and parts of Manitoba, and because providence failed to weep on that land it did not produce the wealth we had been accustomed to see there. The grain was burned up by weather conditions, and the people in that part of the country are hard up to-day principally because they were unable to produce that wealth. That is true in many other lands. It is not possible to put the unemployed to work to remedy that situation. I do not know how many unemployed it would take to water even an acre of wheat. We have no rain producer, like Mr. Hatfield, who came to Alberta and took a good deal of money from the farmers of parts of that province on his undertaking to produce rain. I have no doubt
328	COMMONS
Retiring Allowances-Mr. McLean (Meljort)
my social credit friends are quite sincere; they think they have found something that will be helpful. I hope they have, and that they will have an opportunity to apply it, but the real reason we are poor and hard up is that we have not produced wealth to the extent to which we were accustomed. Take the grain production of the prairie provinces; my hon. friend knows as well as I do that for five or six years we have not produced anything like the amount of grain we formerly did, and as a result we have not had it to sell or exchange for the things we cannot produce ourselves to advantage.
It is another fallacy, I think, to say that this is not an age of scarcity, that we need not suffer for the lack of things we might like to enjoy. Anyone who has produced plenty, who has used it carefully, who has exchanged the surplus for something produced by his neighbour, who has not had too great a toll taken from him by any institution and who has not suffered misfortune, injury or ill health, knows that he is well off.
Another favoured assertion of my hon. friends is that to-day we have an age of machines as against men. This is not an age of machines at all; this is the great age of men, and machines are only the evidence of it, machines that have been made to take over the physical labour, the drudgery, the slavery, the long hours, to take them from the human frame and put them on the machine, where they belong. Do any of my hon. friends think machinery is going to come down from above like manna, that it can be made without physical labour? You cannot find the machinery that is needed in Canada in the drop of ink that lies at the point of a fountain pen. Machines have to be made. Machines do not produce wealth; they simply process further the wealth that men have produced from the resources of nature.
I think my time is almost exhausted, Mr. Speaker, and I wish to thank you and the house for the very courteous reception you have given my argument. It has not been delivered, perhaps, in a very eloquent way, or as clearly as I might like to present it, but when hon. members investigate it they may find that the kernel is there and that if they take advantage of the opportunity of chewing that kernel it will be to their economic enlightenment.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):

Mr. Speaker, the resolution before us looks in the direction of extending the Old Age Pensions Act. It is perhaps rather unfortunate that the administration of that act 
has been transferred from the Department of Labour to the Department of Finance. I suppose the transfer is very natural; the actual administration is so largely under the provinces that so far as the dominion is concerned it is almost entirely a matter of finance, but still I think it puts this kind of legislation in rather an unfortunate position. It makes us think in terms of finance rather than in terms of the needs of the people, and it is to that latter point of view that we should direct our attention to-day.
This is not quite the place or the time to discuss the failings of the present act, but in passing I should like to point out that a great deal of hardship has been caused because of the long residence in Canada that is required. There are many people who came from Great Britain as bona fide settlers who have not lived in this country long enough to qualify under the act. Further, there is an even greater difficulty in Canadian citizens passing from one province to another, which often means that for a good many years they cannot qualify in the province to which they finally removed. I hope the time will come when we will consider Canadian citizens as such irrespective of the actual part of Canada in which they have been living. Again, I think, because of the property qualifications, a good deal of hardship has been caused in the actual administration. A great many people find themselves unable to qualify because of tiny bits of property which perhaps to-day are liabilities rather than assets. In addition we all recognize that the amount of $20 a month is a very, very meagre allowance. I wish that could be increased.
In the resolution now before us we speak of adequate retiring allowances, and there are two points that we should keep in mind. The first is that the amount we give the old people should be adequate to maintain them in a respectable way. It is hardly adequate to-day. Further than that, I am glad to note that my colleague has adopted the phrase "a retiring allowance." As it is to-day, frankly, the old age pension is more or less on a charity basis. I hope the time will come when we will consider that during their working period the older people of this country have done enough work to enable them to claim this allowance as a right rather than as mere charity. You will note, Mr. Speaker, that the resolution links up the necessity for a lower retiring age to the present situation of employment in this country, in these words:
Whereas there exists in Canada an acute unemployment situation-

Retiring Allowances-Mr. Woodsworth
The debates of the house during the last few years will, I think, make clear to anyone that we have had an acute unemployment situation in this country; at the present time some 400,000 people are out of work.
And whereas it is desirable that as many as possible be absorbed into the useful industrial life of the dominion.
The very question that we were discussing on Monday; I do not think it necessary for us to traverse that ground again. Various solutions have been proposed, among others shorter hours. I think that would be a good thing. If there are 400,000 people unemployed there is no reason why the work should not be distributed more equitably so that everyone would have something to do; that is one line of attack. And we have in this resolution a second line of attack, that is reducing the working forces. Now it is quite evident that a good many people at sixty are well able to carry on; on the other hand many people at that age are not in their prime. Surely it would be a good thing if the father should receive a retiring allowance that would take him off the labour market and give that young man a chance to go to work. speechtext: On a question of order, Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask whether the hon. member, who raised the point of order as to myself, is now in order in traversing my argument.

speechtext: I do not think the hon. gentleman is absolutely out of order. Considerable latitude is being given in the treatment of these questions.

subtopic: PROPOSED ALLOWANCES AT AGE SIXTY AND OVER
speechtext:
The arguments of the members opposite, if you can call them such, were put forth long before we called attention to the point of order. I say that we believe there is great potential wealth in this country. Referring to the document of the Brookings Institution which was quoted;, I point out that the consuming power mentioned was limited to what economists call effective demand, that is what the people can pay for. Undoubtedly there never has been any very great surplus over and above what the people can afford to purchase. But if you take another document issued in the United States by a group of economists and technicians, to which I have referred before, that report to the president not long ago clearly showed that if the machinery of production that exists in the United States were used to full capacity it is quite possible to produce the equivalent of $4,400 a year income for every family in the United States. I do not need to go further along that line.
These contentions of ours may be characterized as pseudo-economic theories. I submit, however, that in view of the actual situation and in view of the great need of finding markets for our products, and the huge number of unemployed, it is high time that the Liberals should revise their theories and adopt some plan that would enable them to take care of the present situation. The hon. member for Melfort said that there was no evidence as to the numbers eligible and the cost. That reminds me strongly of the arguments advanced ten years ago when some of us proposed that there should be old age pensions at seventy. It is true that one can make only a guess at these things; that was 
true in England when old age pensions were first proposed, but the population of the different countries conforms to certain general laws, and other countries which have had social legislation of this character for some years are now in a position to advise us as to what the numbers and approximate cost would be. My colleague referred to those figures.
As I have said, there is nothing in the resolution suggesting that any person would be compelled to retire at the age of sixty. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) received a delegation from the Trades and Labour Congress he passed off somewhat lightly the demand made along the lines of this resolution when he suggested that if every person over sixty were bound to retire this would affect both himself and the leader of the delegation, Mr. Draper. That may be quite true. As a gentleman to my right said a few moments ago, it might be that I would have to go, because I have gone beyond the sixty mark. It would probably mean that the Prime Minister would have to go and it would certainly mean that the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) would have to go. But such a pleasantry does not answer the question. Some of us may be able to carry on for a few years longer, especially those of us who have been engaged in intellectual work.
No one wishes to force a man capable of carrying on to retire, although sometimes I think it would be to the advantage of our country if we had a larger proportion of young men in this chamber. We might get some new blood which would bring something of greater value than we have been able to give in the past. I suggest however that such a reply as that given by the Prime Minister does not solve the problem. If some of us were forced to retire, without adequate superannuation, I rather fancy a good many of us might find it extremely difficult to obtain suitable employment. University presidents who are retired at sixty or sixty-five sometimes find it extremely difficult to find other suitable positions. I need not stress that point to hon. members. Any person who has been away from his own profession for ten, fifteen or twenty years and suddenly finds himself thrown out, without any reserve, would, even though intellectually acute and able, find himself in grave difficulties w'hen he went about securing another position. I have known only too many people who have been in that position.
I am not thinking however so much of the intellectual workers, but rather of the

Retiring Allowances-Mr. Woodsworth
manual labourers. To-day in many industries men are being laid off not at sixty but at fifty, and sometimes forty years. Certainly no man is taken on in ordinary industry after he has reached fifty years of age. A great many people find themselves in very distressing conditions when at sixty years they are laid aside and cannot hope to obtain old age pensions until they reach the age of seventy. I would call the attention of hon. members to the fact that with the exception of the farming population five-sixths of the working class population in Canada are employees. That means that with the wages they have been receiving they have had no opportunity to lay up very much by way of reserves. Further, we know there is a considerable turnover in the personnel in nearly all our factories, which means that many of our people may have worked in ten, twenty, thirty or forty different establishments between the ages of, shall we say sixteen and sixty. No one particular establishment has any responsibility for such an employee who reaches old age. The last firm which employed him has no special responsibility when he reaches the time he must retire. Some employers who may have a greater sense of responsibility and are more humane than others may seek to keep employees in their service after they have passed the period of greatest efficiency. There should be some general provision, however, and industry as a whole, or the state, should have the responsibility of seeing that a man who has done good work between the ages of sixteen or eighteen and sixty should be decently looked after in his older days.
There is nothing very radical in the resolution, notwithstanding the observations of the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. McLean). There is nothing particularly socialistic in it. I say it is an honest effort fairly to meet one of the outstanding practical and personal problems facing us to-day. I would hope that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), who since this affects his department will undoubtedly reply, would give the matter serious consideration. The resolution is not offered by way of criticizing the government for what it has not done in the past. We have a new government to-day. The resolution is not put forward as a result of any special theory, unless it be this, that the needs of Canadian citizens should have priority, and that in a country potentially as rich as Canada there is no reason for elderly people suffering hardship. That is our plea for reducing the age at which old age pension or retiring allowance may be received.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with your kind permission, before saying a few words about the subject under discussion may I offer congratulations to the hon. member for West Kootenay (Mr. Esling) upon passing another milestone in life. Perhaps I may be permitted also to express the hope that he has many years ahead of him and that many of them will be spent, not on this but on the other side of the chamber.
I would not intrude into this debate did I not realize and appreciate that a new member making his initial effort is given every possible consideration by older members who have had more experience. My main reason for taking part in this discussion is my long experience with young men and young women. I concur with the mover of the resolution (Mr. Heaps) in his expression of sympathy for the young men and women of this country because of the position in which they find themselves to-day. That position is not of their own making; they have been called upon to suffer intensely because of conditions prevailing at the present time. I gained further encouragement from listening to the very able address made earlier this week by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers). I offer him my sincere congratulations upon his address. I hope that some of the principles which he enunciated will be brought down in the form of legislation in the very near future so that we shall have something concrete to discuss and not have to continue to deal with abstract problems.
For the past eight years we have been going through a period of distress, but this is not the first time in the history of the world that a period of distress has overcome us. I look back to the latter part of the seventeenth century when our forefathers were changing over from hand to machine labour and think of the distress that followed in the wake of that change. I look back to the social revolution that followed immediately the change in the economic life of the people of that time. Conditions which prevailed then were similar to those which have prevailed during our own lifetime. We have seen a remarkable economic change in the adoption of electrically driven machines and other types of machinery which have largely relieved man of heavy labour. Between the industrial and social revolutions occurred the Napoleonic wars which aggravated a rather unfortunate situation. In our own day the great war accentuated conditions which would have occurred even though the war had

not taken place. We are in the midst of change and we must readjust the social fabric of this country to meet the changes that have taken and are now taking place. The main trouble and difficulty in Canada is the fact that compared with other countries of the world we are many years behind in social legislation. We have not kept up with the economic and industrial changes which have occurred during the past twenty-five years.
I should like to point out one peculiar fact in connection with conditions which prevail in this country. During the early part of this century we entered upon a period of tremendous expansion. I recall the words of that great Canadian statesman, a man who led this house for many years, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, when he said that the nineteenth century belonged to the United States of America, but the twentieth century would belong to Canada. That statement was true then and is true to-day; the only difficulty is that we started to build on the expectation of an immediate realization of that statement. The development of Canadla has been impeded by the war and by industrial conditions which developed after Sir Wilfrid made that statement. We are overdeveloped in our railway system; we are overdeveloped in our industrial system ; we are overdeveloped in our governmental system, and the result is that we find ourselves unable to cope with a situation which at its best would have been bad enough but which was further aggravated by this period of tremendous expansion.
We have considerable unemployment in our midst to-day. The other evening the remark was made from the other side of the house that unemployment began to be felt only after 1930. Unemployment actually made its presence felt in this country in 1925; it was only accentuated and forced upon our attention in 1930. Government reports show that in the heyday of our prosperity, in 1928, the number of unemployed in Canada was actually 146,000 people. That figure did not take into account those who are usually unemployed, such as the indigent class which we have with us always, or those who are seasonally unemployed. The figure shows that the unemployment situation began to develop long before 1930 when it was brought home to us so forcibly.
It would be useless for me to attempt to inquire into all the various causes and reasons which might be advanced for the depression out of which we are striving to find our way at the present time. It will be sufficient for me to direct the attention of hon. members to some figures. Lack of income on the part

Retiring Allowances-Mr. Deachman
of our Canadian citizens is responsible to a large degree for the over supply of materials and commodities with which we find ourselves. I notice that in 1929 the total income of the Canadian people was $5,500,000,000; in 1932 this had shrunk to $3,181,000,000. a shrinkage of over two billion dollars. When you take out of circulation in this country a purchasing power of over two billion dollars the natural consequence is a lack of employment and a lack of ability on the part of the people to get the wherewithal with which to enjoy life.
There is another point I should like to raise, one with which all hon. members on this side may not agree. A year ago my faith in the Conservative party was emphasized and reestablished in no uncertain degree by the series of addresses given by our leader. The statements that he made at that time were implemented by measures passed by the house, which measures represented considerable progress in social legislation. It is my hope and expectation that something further will be done along that line and that the legislation passed last year will be found to be in order and will be supplemented by additional legislation introduced at this session by the present government. We are in dire need of advanced social legislation; the Canadian people are clamouring for that type of legislation, and rightly so. I feel that they have a right to demand it, for in my opinion it is the first duty of the state to provide for the sustenance of the people living within it. The statement I wanted to make, with which many members might disagree, I would put in these words: We have reached a point where we know there is a surplus of labour. I am going to say this, and I am open to contradiction and correction if I am wrong in my line of reasoning and the conclusions I have reached: Never again in the history of Canada are we going to have a balanced budget in respect to labour conditions in this country. There will always be a surplus of labour in the labour market not only of Canada but of the world, and for that reason I am keenly urging that some action be taken in relation to social legislation in order to meet a necessity which has arisen and is bound to remain with us. This surplus of labour must be looked after; it is	our duty to look after every
class of citizen living in Canada. And these people can be taken care of only by means of legislation such as is proposed in the motion before us and legislation of a similar type.
As I said in the first place, I am expecting great things from the new Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers). Although he sits on the opposite side, I admire his capacity; I know his ability and I feel that if he is given a free hand by other members on his side of the house he will bring in legislation that will tend to alleviate some of the distress with which we are faced at the present time.
In conclusion I wish to emphasize this fact as forcibly as I can: Social legislation must immediately be introduced and we must take cognizance of the fact that there is a surplus of labour in the labour market; we must take cognizance of the fact that there will always be a surplus of labour, and we must adjust our social legislation to meet a circumstance of that kind.

subtopic: PROPOSED ALLOWANCES AT AGE SIXTY AND OVER
speechtext:
The resolution brought forward by the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) will not increase the total number of men employed. One section of the working army is to be retired and a new section is to take its place, but the unit strength of that army will remain the same. It will not increase the total amount of production and therefore will not increase the total amount of purchasing power. I go further: it will decrease the wages paid.
My friends are a bit uncertain as to the cost, one mentioned a total army of 870,000 which was to be retired, and another suggested a payment of $50 a month or $600 a year. There would therefore be a total bill to meet of $120,000,000 a year. That sum must be met; it must be paid out of total production, and therefore there will be a smaller total to distribute, and as a result a lower net or real wage going to the worker. I go further; it will decrease the total number of men employed, for the simple reason that when you add a burden of this kind you have greater taxes to pay; and in the matter of taxation there is even now in the dominion a burden too great to be borne. Certain industries under pressure now would decline, fail and go out of business.
It would add a greater burden to the industries which are competitive in the export market of the world, and therefore they would not be able to produce in the same volume as before, and so there would be a decline in the total number of men employed.
I know that my hon. friends who have spoken this afternoon represent largely the labour interests. It is most astounding that we should see standing up in this house to-day leading representatives of labour bringing forward a proposal, which can do nothing but reduce the wages of the employee and decrease the total number of men employed. I wonder if this is the greatest constructive

Retiring Allowances-Mr. Maclnnis
suggestion they can offer. I leave that baby on their doorstep; it is their own. I ask them, if the opportunity comes and they may have the chance, to explain in what way this is going to improve the position of the worker, either in so far as numbers are concerned or as regards the wages paid to the individual.

subtopic: PROPOSED ALLOWANCES AT AGE SIXTY AND OVER
speechtext:
In seconding this resolution proposed by the hon .member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps), I felt that I was merely supporting a resolution that would direct a certain matter to the attention of the government, asking that a certain principle should receive consideration. We did not nor could we lay down the exact terms in which this matter could be carried into legislation. That ,vill be the function of the government if ind when they feel that the resolution has merit. Before going any further I wish to quote very briefly from a statement made by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in this house in the session of 1925, which can be found in Hansard of that year. Old age pensions were being discussed at the time, and this is what the present Prime Minister, who was also at that time Prime Minister, said:
There is need for society to assist in the protection of its members against a condition which simultaneously places Durdens upon the workers whose day's work is done, and>
on the worker whose day's work is just beginning. If the young are to be given a fair start in life, the care of the aged should not be their first responsibility.
That principle holds true to-day in a far greater degree than in 1925, because the conditions that exist to-day, which put a greater responsibility on the young as well as on the aged, are intensified. There was never a time when it was more necessary than it is to-day to make provision for people for whom industry has no use. There was never a time when this could be more easily done, because there was never a time when the means and the material with which to do it was as great as it is to-day.
The hon. gentleman who has just sat down (Mr. Deachman) asks whether we have taken the expense into consideration. Yes, we have taken expenses into consideration, and we know what they are. All the expenses involved are the labour it requires to bring those material things into being. All other expenses are merely those that arise because of the property relationship that exists in human society to-day. When one set of people own and another set of people do not own, every single item that enters into the lives of those who do not own must come

out of the property and income of those who do. So as long as this property relation exists the question of expense will be always with us. But once we overcome that question of property, the matter of expense will disappear, and we can go on and develop the resources of this country so as to provide not only for the necessities of life but for the comforts and luxuries as well. To-day, because of the profit system, the masses of the people are living in poverty, in misery and in insecurity in the midst of plenty. That is the situation.
So far as we in this corner of the house are concerned, we ask the government to do, not the limit that we should like to see done, not the things that we believe are possible to be done, but the things that we believe are within the ambit of their own program. That is where we stand on the matter. I have been a member of the working class all my life. I know that there are many men to-day over the age of sixty who would be very glad to retire on a pension of much less than fifty dollars a month. I know also that there are many people in industry whom their employers are keeping at work, although they realize that their industrial efficiency is gone. There are various reasons for this. In some cases they do not wish to throw them on the scrap heap of unemployment; in others, some protection is afforded to the employee by trade union regulations and such things as that. Recently the province of British Columbia made a survey of unemployment in that province. It shows very clearly how unemployment increases with advancing age. In examining figures for a ten year period experts find that there are 4,300 persons on relief between twenty and thirty years of age, 5,188 between thirty and forty, 5,636 between forty and fifty, 6,526 between fifty and sixty and 4,345 between sixty and seventy. I think that gives an indication of how difficult it is for people who are getting up in years to find employment in industry at the present time. In British Columbia employers in the lumbering and fishing industries do not want men over the age of thirty-five. In the lumber industry they can get all the active young men they want below that age. I visited quite a. number of plants in British Columbia this year, particularly the works of the Consolidated Mining & Smelting Company in Trail, and it was really amazing to note the youth of the employees as a whole. It appeared to me that there was not a man over fifty years of age working in the whole of that huge plant.

Retiring Allowances-Mr. Maclnnis
Something must be done to take care of these people. The hon. member for Melfort (Mr. McLean) said that the means of overcoming the situation that confronted us today was quite simple. All we had to do was to go on producing all we could produce and then clear away trade barriers and exchange our surplus goods for the surpluses of other nations. That is quite a reasonable and a logical thing to do. But the fact of the matter is that it cannot be done; that is, it cannot be done at the present time and under the present system. Let us take as an example the largest free trade area in the world. The United States of America, with its 130 million people and with an enormous territory where they are capable of producing almost every known commodity, is to-day the largest free trade area in the world, and if free trade in itself could effectively distribute the fruits of industry, why are there eleven million people unemployed in the United States? Why are there approximately 21 million in the United States on relief? You cannot settle the question by declaring that it can be solved simply through clearing away trade barriers. The reason it cannot be done in that way is that certain people in the world to-day, even in the Dominion of Canada, are receiving so much of the total pool of production that they do not know what to do with it; they could not exchange it and use the commodities that they could get in exchange even though they wanted to do so.
During 1934 and 1935 we had a commission sitting on price spreads and mass buying. I am not going to take up the time of the house with any extensive discussion of this report, but I would like to call your attention to one of the industries investigated at that time. It was found that the average wages in the tobacco industry were $555 a year. Reference was made in the investigation of one of the tobacco firms to others beside the workers who produce the wealth by manufacturing the raw material into saleable commodities:	others were getting income as
well. The president, Gray Miller, was receiving in those years of depression, from 1929 to 1933, $25,000 a year. Besides that salary he received as a bonus in 1929, over $45,000; in 1930, over $61,000; in 1931, over $40,000; in 1932, over $32,000, and in 1933, over $44,000. How can people receiving incomes of that size exchange the values which that income represents and consume the values received in exchange? It cannot be done. Going on a little further: the vice-president, D. C. Patterson, was receiving a salary of $40,000 a year. Compare that with the average wage
of the employees, $555 a year. And besides that salary of $40,000 he received a bonus each year: in 1929 it was $75,000; in 1930 it was $102,000; in 1931 it was over $67,000 and in 1932 it was over $53,000. Do you wonder that there is a surplus of commodities that cannot be consumed, although there are people who are ready to consume them?
Now I shall take up another tobacco manufacturing plant, the Macdonald manufacturing plant.

It would take an individual employee of that factory 468 years to take out of the industry as much as the owner took out in one year. That is where the money can be found. I do not find very much fault with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) for trying to stop the discussion there, because it does not look very well, but still these things will have to become known.
