Retiring Allowances-Mr. Church
that the government will take this matter into consideration, having in mind not merely the wording of the resolution but also its intent. If they cannot go all the way I am sure that those of us in the little group in this corner will be very grateful if they can go any distance at all.

subtopic: PROPOSED ALLOWANCES AT AGE SIXTY AND OVER
speechtext:
Mr
Speaker, I am opposed to the proposal enunciated in this resolution; I am opposed to putting any more burdens or artificial barriers on business to-day in the two industrial provinces of Canada. The other night, it is true, I did support the expenditure of public money, and I am prepared to support it again. Today we are spending $100,000,000 on relief in this country, federal, provincial and municipal, and it was shown before the housing committee last year that about two-thirds of that amount, or $60,000,000, if distributed among the carpenters, bricklayers and labourers of all kinds in wages would get thousands of people off the dole and back to work. I believe an economic arrangement of that kind could be made.
Let us have a look at the cause and effect of this resolution. It is simply state socialism, to which I am absolutely opposed. I do not think it will afford the unemployed any more relief than the special academic pleading of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) the other night, when he had before him the example of England and the United States as to what could be done in regard to reconstruction and housing within the ability of this country to pay. This question of unemployment is a matter exclusively for this parliament. Here we make the tariff, the immigration laws, the banking and commerce laws and so on, and for that reason we must be responsible for unemployment. One of the glories of the Victorian era was the fact that the people kept the state. If the socialists both in and out of this house go much further it will be a case of the state keeping the people, first, last and all the time. William Pitt was prime minister of Great Britain at twenty-three-
A sight to make surrounding nations stare,
A kingdom entrusted to a schoolboy's care.
-but every age does not produce a Pitt.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, this resolution would have the very opposite effect to what I think is intended by the mover (Mr. Heaps). I am sorry I did not bring down with me the return asked for by the late Mr. McCrea, an old member of the house for Sherbrooke, which showed that eighty per cent of the cash taxes of this dominion were paid by the two central provinces. The heavy burdens and artificial barriers placed upon business to-day in Ontario and Quebec are driving

many business men to the wall and are one of the main causes of unemployment and unrest. Let me say to my socialist friends that the right to possess private property such as a job is derived from nature, not from the state or from man. That is a principle that has been known for many years, and is not the title to a job property? This parliament of Canada and the state has no authority to abolish that right, but only to control its use and bring it into harmony with the public good. The state has no right to abolish private property; a man's job is his private property, and the government has no right to take that away from him.
Last year the party to which I belong provided a new deal and a new future for the people. I cannot speak for this corner of the house officially all or any of the time but I can say that we are just as much opposed to state socialism as we are to the laissez-faire policy of the Liberty party and to economic liberalism and state and social credit socialism. As it is, this country is burdened with debt to an almost impossible extent owing to the war and the cost of daily increasing social services, so that we are threatened with a condition in which no one would be working and the state would have to keep not some of the people some of the time but all of the people all of the time. We are consistent protectionists; we believe in protection all the time for all the people, not some of the people some of the time. We favour protection for the iron, the coal and steel industries for the farmer and for all classes, and for the industrial worker who is foreclosed, the same as the farmer and fisherman. Who but the former Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) would have done the work he did. for this country for the past five years? What man of sixty or under could have done this so efficiently? This party is just as much opposed to economic socialism as we are to the economics of the Manchester school and economic liberalism held by the Minister of Labour. We do not want mob coercion. Modern capitalism shares a great deal of the blame for economic conditions in this country and must clean house and adopt a new set of rules-every living game has to have new rules from time to time and the capitalistic system requires a new set of rules to bring it up to date. But in any system the principle must be retained of every man working for himself, instead of state socialism as called for in this resolution. We in this country will never become slaves; the state will never take away our freedom. We must cure these evils of unrestricted competition, starvation wages,

Retiring Allowances-Mr. Church
sweat shops, long hours, monopolies, child labour and all such things; we should ibe better employed in giving our attention to these matters rather than to the proposed resolution, which will get us nowhere and destroy every industry in central Canada which pays the 'bills mainly for all Canada.
Who is going to pay for all this? It would just go on the taxes of the industrial provinces and industry would practically have to close up. This whole idea started about twenty years ago. Most of us remember a distinguished citizen of Toronto, Sir William Osier, who graduated from McGill and went to the great Johns Hopkins hospital in Baltimore and became professor of clinical medicine there and afterwards went to Oxford. The hon. members for West York (Mr. Streight) and North York (Mr. Mulock) represent the ridings in which the father of this celebrated man lived. In 1905 Sir William Osier made a speech in which he said that men at forty are inefficient and at sixty are useless. That has since been proven to be wrong; the war proved it wrong, and conditions after the war have proved it wrong. If we took away from the arts and sciences, from literature and medicine what the men over forty or even over sixty did, we should be back in the middle ages. Of course there are exceptions. Sir William Osier's idea was that the man over sixty is settled in a rigid mental groove so that he no longer has imagination enough to develop new ideas and adjust himself to new conditions. Henry Ford declared recently that men of middle age are stable and experienced and do better work, calling for endurance, which is often shirked by younger men. Had the experience and judgment of the older men been heeded in 1929 the world might have been saved some of the consequences of the stock crash disaster. They gave warning against the vast speculation. The value of their judgment is incalculable, especially in industrial affairs. If all the men over sixty were withdrawn from the financial institutions, banks and insurance companies and labour generally in this country, I do not know what would become of it.
The first duty of the government is to solve the problem of unemployment and distribution and I regret that the government of the day in the speech from the throne have not brought down some measures for the help of what Disraeli called the suffering millions. Those people-the entire working classes- have little to hope for from the statement of the purely academic Minister of Labour in this house the other evening. If that is the best that twentieth century liberalism which put him in the cabinet can do, we have little to
hope for from them. I have studied this matter for some time. Twentieth century liberalism is content to sit back and 'leave these great economic problems to solve themselves. The young Minister of Labour the other night gave a learned treatise of special pleading which might well have been delivered to a mock parliament or in a debate between McGill, Queens, and Varsity, and his announcement to the unemployed was: We can do nothing. Etconomic liberalism calls for wider markets, which are not available in a world in which there is only economic nationalism. Where are the jobs to come from? Instead of having a real labour man to find jobs in Canada for Canadians, are we to continue the policy of the government that was in power from 1921 to 1930, when over 750,000 young men had to go to the United States to find jobs, many of them returned soldiers who had fought for this country in France and Flanders, at the hazard of their lives, owing to the free trade policies of the government of the day.
In conclusion I want to read a few words bearing on this subject from an article in the English Review for November. The editor of this magazine is a noted economist in the old land, the famous Douglas Jerrold. The writer says:
As examples of physical as well as mental strength in old age, we have Von Moltke, who was chief of staff of the Prussian army at eighty-eight; John Wesley, who was constantly travelling and who preached almost daily at the same age; and Gladstone, who began his reat Midlothian campaign at eighty, and ecame prime minister, for the fourth time, at eighty-three. Two great artists and a noted actor close the record of aged yet efficient workers. Michel Angelo at eighty-nine was busily engaged on his immortal frescoes; that other master, Titian, painted his Battle of Lepanto at ninety-eight, and Charles Macklin, the Shakespearean actor, performed at Covent Garden theatre as Macbeth at eighty-four and as Shylock at ninety-nine.
The list of the mentally virile in old age is fairly lengthy; too long to quote with any approximation _ to completeness, but a few instances extending into our own times may be added.... Among soldiers the most notable were Lord Roberts, and Marechals Joffre and Foch.
Referring to Thomas Edison, the article states he died in 1931 at the age of 84. He produced inventions that benefited the whole world when he was well past 60 and worked in his laboratory till his last illness:
He declared that a man ought to "work with increasing efficiency" between thirty-six and sixty. Robert Dollar, the founder of the Dollar steamship lines, who died recently at the age of eighty-eight, was convinced he had accomplished more in his later years than before he had reached sixty. Of those still with us, and still at work, the most prominent,



Retiring Allowances-Mr. Douglas
perhaps, are President Masaryk. the efficient head of the Czechoslovakian Republic, now eighty-four, Mr. Henry Ford, the poet Rabindranath Tagore (who is still busy conducting his college at Shantiniketan), and that outstanding example of indefatigable physical and mental energy, George Bernard Shaw, who, vigorous at seventy-four, recently circumnavigated the world. His opinion of Sir William Osier's incautious ana unreasonable condemnation of all above forty, as partially or wholly incapable, has not, I think, been made public, but it would be worth hearing.
At another point the article reads:
Bacon, it is said, outlined his Novum Organum at the age of fifteen-a statement difficult to believe-but completed it for publication at fifty-nine. Kant wrote his Estimate of Living Force at twenty-three, but published his Critique of Pure Reason when fifty-seven. Handel and Meyerbeer, both precocious composers, wrote, the former his oratorio The Triumph of Time, at seventy-two; and the latter, at the same age, produced his opera, L'Africaine. Verdi, at seventy-one, composed his masterpiece, Othello, and his other brilliant work, Falstaff, in his eightieth year. Isaac Disraeli published his Amenities of Literature at seventy-five, at which age Bismarck was deposed from his chancellorship by the egotistical ex-Kaiser. Victor Hugo, at seventy-five, wrote The History of Crime; at seventy-seven Le Pape; at seventy-eight, L'Ane; at seventy-nine, Les Quartre Vents de l'Esprit; and at eighty, Torquemada. Humboldt began to write at seventy-six his great work Kosmos. and finished it at eighty. Lamarck completed his famous zoological treatise, the Natural History of the Invertebrates at seventy-eight. Goethe completed his Faust when eighty, and Ranke commenced at this advanced age his History of the World, and actually lived to complete it. He died at ninety-one. Tennyson was eighty-three when he wrote Crossing the Bar. Walter Savage Landor -wrote his Imaginary Conversations at eighty-five.
What right has the mover of the resolution, an hon. member of the house, to interfere with industry in this way? Why should the house pass a resolution of this kind without first knowing how industries stand? Only last session we had information as to the number of unemployed in the country. We would have to see the cause and effect of the suggested change, and I suggest the cause and effect would not be that which the mover suggests. If we were to develop our natural resources, the products of the sea, the soil, the forests and the mines, there would be work for everybody. A few nights ago I referred to what the Hon. Miss Perkins, Secretary of Labor in Washington, has done for the high school population. In Denmark high schools have been erected which will give adult education and will have the effect of creating work. When speaking on Monday of this week I referred to a former president of the board of education, sitting as a member of the Baldwin government, and

indicated he had said that within three years there would be an agricultural economic revolution in the old world, Lord Eustace Percy.
I do not wish to assume responsibility for talking this resolution out, which I can do in three minutes more, because undoubtedly some reply will have to be made by the government. I will state, however, that we should consider seriously cause and effect. Legislation such as is suggested in the resolution would involve greater taxes, and would amount to a restraint of trade and commerce and increase unemployment a hundredfold. I would state further that the government should consider seriously the problem of unemployment, because it is the most important one before us. The very basis of society is at stake, unless we find some up to date solution.
I am in favour of liberal pensions for those who are incapacitated, but I do not favour pensions for people such as I have mentioned, people who are efficient and who are able to work for many years after they have reached the age of sixty. I do not believe there is any demand or agitation from industry that the resolution be accepted. I should like to hear from labour unions and business men before the government would accept the suggestion contained therein.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am quite prepared to assume responsibility for talking this resolution out. I rise to support the resolution proposed by the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps). I trust however that we shall not have an organization such as that existing in the United States, because I would hate to see a Heaps plan with the slogan, "everybody for Heaps and heaps for everybody."
I have been amazed this afternoon to hear the variety of subtle objections raised to the resolution. Naturally I expected there would be an objection to the expenditure of the large sum of money involved, but I was more amazed to hear some of the other objections voiced. For instance I was surprised to hear the last speaker deal with state socialism when, after all, the reform suggested in the resolution has been in effect in Denmark since 1861, at which time there was a beginning of a system of non-contributory pensions. If I remember correctly, listening to the radio speeches of the right hon. leader (Mr. Bennett) of the last speaker I heard him make a proposition very similar to the one contained in the resolution. It was similar at least in some of the details and would have helped the same people.

Bureau for Translations-Mr. Pouliot
The hon. member for North Huron (Mr. Deachman) made an even stranger objection. If I remember correctly he left the baby on our doorstep; I hope the hon. member will not make that a habit, because it is a most unbecoming one. The suggestion he made that we were advocating lower wages and a decrease in employment and production is beside the point, in view of the fact that in 1927 the party to which he belongs, headed by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) suggested this very thing, but with an increased age limit. In the present instance we are asking simply that the age limit be lowered and the amount increased; we are not asking for state socialism or for any legislation which would increase unemployment. It seems to me therefore that the arguments advanced by these hon. gentlemen have been beside the point. The hon. member for Melfort (Mr. McLean), too, advanced some objections.
